questions.text: A6 compares each pod's logged version ids to those from A4. Which log line shows a pod's version ids, given R1 does not say it logs them and R2 only logs when a secret changes?
questions.about: A6. Confirm every instance is on the new keys

questions.text: Why must A6 wait one refresh interval after the last A4 write if new pods read the latest version at startup anyway? Which pods does that wait apply to?
questions.about: A6, At least one refresh interval (5 minutes), plus a margin

questions.text: What is the managed secret store here (which product), and what is the pod's 'workload identity'? How does a pod get it without a credential in an env var?
questions.about: R1. Startup load, Store auth uses the pod's workload identity

questions.text: The new key is in the store from A4, but the old image still serves traffic until A5. If someone writes another version in the store before A5, what do new pods load, and does the A6 check still match?
Who runs each step (A0 to A10)? Who approves the A5 merge and deploys it, given engineers have no prod read access?
In R3, after a 401/403 triggers an out-of-band refresh, how does the request that got the 401 end? Does the customer see an error?
How does the developer's own identity get dev access, and does `make run --offline` skip R1 completely? How does the app know to use the stub server?
What exactly does the readiness probe check after R1: a flag set once all three secrets are loaded? And what does 'passes the new readiness probe' mean for the rollout timing in A5?

answers.text: The plan now names the lines. R1 logs `secret loaded name=<name> version=<id> pod=<pod>` once per secret at startup, and R2 logs `secret rotated` on change. A6 reads each pod's latest of these lines per name. A pod that never rotated shows its startup line, which is enough. Changed in R1, R2 and A6.

The wait applies to pods that loaded an older version before the last store write. A pod that started after that write already has the newest version and needs no wait. In the planned sequence all new-image pods start after A4, so the wait is a margin for any later write. It lets each refresher run once after the last write, so A6 does not depend on timing luck. Changed in A6.

The brief does not name the secret store product, and it does not say how a pod gets its workload or service identity without an environment credential. deploy.md says pods run under `orders-api-prod`. The plan now says the platform provides the identity and lists both points as Open question 11. The platform owner must confirm them.

R1 says new pods load the latest version at startup. So if someone writes a newer version before A5, new pods load that one, and an A6 check against the A4 ids would fail even though the pods are right. A6 now compares each pod with the latest store version at check time, and any write during the rollout is logged in the migration log. Changed in A4 and A6.

Known from the brief: the security on-call writes prod secrets and performs the A4 writes, and engineers have no prod read. Not known: who runs A0, A1, A2, A5 (merge and deploy), A6 and A7, and who approves the A5 merge. The brief does not assign these. Added as Open question 10.

The request that gets a 401 or 403 fails with the provider's error, as it does today. It is not retried with another key. The out-of-band refresh only helps later requests. Customers should see this only if a revoked key is in memory, and A6 and A7 prevent that before any revocation. Changed in R3.

Developers reach dev through the A1 policy, which gives engineers read and write on dev only. `make run --offline` skips R1 entirely. The flag tells the app to point each provider client at the local stub server and to use a fixed dummy key in memory. `ready` is set at once, so readiness still works. Simplest handling, and it never touches prod. Changed in R4 and R6.

Readiness checks a `ready` flag, which is set once R1 has loaded all three secrets (R4). In A5, 'passes the readiness probe' means the probe returns 200, which happens only after R1 succeeds. The rollout waits on that before it stops an old pod, so a pod that cannot load keys never gets traffic. Changed in R4.

questions.text: A0 lists cron jobs, other services and CI jobs that use the live keys. What happens to them in A5 and A6? Do they move to the store too, and who confirms they are on the new keys before A7?
What counts as an unknown consumer being found in A0? How does A0 find consumers whose use of the key is not written down, and when is A0 considered finished?
questions.about: A7. Revoke the old keys, one provider at a time

questions.text: Who reads the central log and compares the version ids to the store, given engineers cannot read prod values? Can they see version ids, and is the check done by hand or by a script?
questions.about: A6. Confirm every instance is on the new keys

questions.text: How does the deploy tooling know an image tag was built before the migration commit? What does an engineer see when they try such a rollback during an incident?
questions.about: A8. Block rollback to pre-migration images

questions.text: Between A4 and A6, can a pod's cache hold a new key that the provider rejects (a bad key written in A4)? How is that spotted before A7, given readiness only checks loading?
In the old image path of A5, the old pods never refresh. Does the new image's refresher only matter for later rotations, and is it needed at all for this migration's A6 check?

answers.text: Cron jobs, other services and CI jobs are not covered by A5 or A6, which check pods only. The plan now says each non-pod consumer must either stop using the live key or be confirmed on the new key by its owner before A7 for that key. It gets no prod read from this plan. How it is confirmed, and whether it needs its own identity, is not decided (Open question 12).

An unknown consumer is any use of a live key that is not on the A0 list. A0 finds them by searching the repos, CI config and config history for the three key names and the provider base URLs, by asking each service and job owner, and by checking per-key usage where the provider shows it. A0 is finished when every listed consumer has an owner who has confirmed the entry. Whether a watch window is also needed is open (Open question 12). Changed in A0.

Log lines carry only names and version ids (R5). Version ids are not secret values, so engineers can read the log lines. The comparison is a script, a saved log query plus a store lookup, not a manual check. The security on-call runs the store side, because it already holds prod access. Whether an engineer can see version ids without value read is not known (Open question 11). Changed in A6.

Not known: which deploy tool is used, and whether image tags record the build commit. The plan states the rule: refuse any image built from a commit before the migration commit, which needs the build commit recorded per image. The plan defines no override path, so an engineer in an incident gets a refusal and no defined next step. The message wording and any exception route are not known (Open question 3 and 7). Changed in A8.

Yes. A4 writes a new key that the provider might reject, and a new pod loads it at startup, so requests routed to that pod can fail with 401 or 403. That breaks the no-customer-failure rule. The plan now (a) validates each new key with a provider read-only check before the A4 write where one exists, and (b) in A5 holds the rollout when the new pods' 401/403 rate is above the old pods' rate. Without (a), (b) is the only guard, and some requests may fail before the rollout halts (Open question 5). Changed in A4 and A5.

The refresher is not needed for the A5 cutover itself, because new pods read the latest version at startup. Old pods never refresh, which is why A6 requires that no old-image pod remains. The refresher matters for later rotations, and for the A6 margin when a store write happens during the rollout. Changed in R2.

teachbacks.text:
Walkthrough: one key (payments_api_key) followed from "leaked key in config" to "old key revoked", then the runtime path inside a pod.

1. Starting point. The three provider keys (payments, email, geocoding) are currently in config/*.yaml, and the client copies the key in its constructor. The keys are in git history and history is not rewritten. So every key gets rotated at its provider, and the new values go in a managed secret store at orders-api/<env>/<name>, where <env> is prod or dev. Each store write creates a version id.

2. A0, inventory. Once the plan is approved, nothing changes in the system. People list every live consumer of the keys: pods, cron jobs, other services, CI jobs and developer machines. They find them by searching repos, CI config and config history for the key names and provider URLs, by asking owners, and by checking provider usage per key. The result is a migration log of names and locations, with no key values. A0 is done when each listed consumer has an owner who confirmed it. If an unknown consumer turns up later, it blocks revoking that key (A7) but not A1 to A6.

3. A1, provision. After A0, infrastructure-as-code creates the dev and prod store paths and one KMS key per environment. It also defines IAM:
   - The `orders-api-prod` identity can only read orders-api/prod/*.
   - The security on-call can write prod. Value read is removed if the store can split read from write.
   - Engineers can read and write dev only.
   - The CI deploy identity cannot read prod values.
   If the IaC apply fails, nothing changes. A policy simulation checks the result.

4. A2, dev. Sandbox keys go into orders-api/dev/*. `make run` sets APP_ENV=dev and reads dev secrets with the developer's own identity. Per-environment base URLs mean dev uses sandbox URLs. Providers with no sandbox key use `make run --offline`. A5 must not merge until A2 is verified.

5. A3, new keys. With security on-call approval, new keys are issued at each provider. The old keys stay valid. The new keys go only to the security on-call, through an approved channel. If a provider cannot issue a key, stop. Prod is untouched.

6. A4, write to prod. The security on-call writes each new key to orders-api/prod/<name>. If the provider has a read-only auth check, the key is checked first. A failed check means no write. Each write returns a version id, and the id (not the value) goes in the migration log. Running pods still hold the old keys and the old image does not read the store, so traffic is unchanged. A failed write changes nothing and is retried.

7. A5, ship the new image. The change is reviewed and merged to main, and CI builds the image. The new code loads the three secrets at startup, has a readiness probe that waits for that load, removes the api_key lines from config/app.yaml, and includes the CI guard (A9). The deploy is rolling with maxUnavailable: 0, so a new pod must pass readiness before an old pod stops. Old pods hold old keys and new pods hold new keys, and both are valid. The rollout continues only while the 401/403 rate on new pods is at or below that of old pods. Failure cases:
   - A new pod that cannot reach the store exits non-zero and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and the old pods keep serving.
   - A new pod with a key the provider rejects does become ready, because readiness checks loading and not validity. The gate catches it and halts the rollout. Some requests may fail before the halt. The fix is to redeploy the previous image, which still has valid old keys.

8. What a new pod does at startup (R1). `main` makes an explicit call. For each secret it reads the latest version of orders-api/<APP_ENV>/<name>, using the pod's platform-provided service identity and a bounded timeout. On success it logs `secret loaded name version pod`. It makes 4 attempts in total: one try, then 3 retries 2 seconds apart. "Not found" is fatal immediately. If all attempts fail, it logs the failing secret names and error types, then exits non-zero. When all three have loaded, the in-memory `ready` flag is set. Values live only in the SecretCache, a map of name to (value, version_id, fetched_at). Entries are swapped whole.

9. Readiness and liveness (R4). The readiness probe returns 200 only when `ready` is set. A later refresh failure does not clear it. Liveness returns 200 while the process runs and does not depend on the store. This is how the A5 rollout stays safe.

10. A customer request (R3). A request that needs a provider reads the key from the cache at call time, and the client no longer copies it at construction. The store is never called on the request path, so a store outage does not affect requests. If the provider answers 401 or 403, the request fails with the provider's error and is not retried. A WARNING is logged with the version id and the error code, and one out-of-band refresh is triggered, limited to once per 60 seconds. That refresh does not help the failed request.

11. Background refresh (R2). Every 5 minutes, with jitter, each pod reads the latest version of each secret. If the version id is unchanged, nothing happens. If it changed, the pod checks that the value is non-empty with no whitespace, swaps the cache entry, and logs `secret rotated`. On any failure it keeps the last good value, logs a WARNING and tries again next time. A separate alert fires when `fetched_at` is stale past a threshold that ops choose. This refresh is not needed for the A5 cutover. It matters for later rotations and for the A6 margin.

12. Logging (R5). Logs carry only the secret name and version id. The secret value type prints as `<redacted>`. Authorization headers and request bodies are kept out of exceptions and HTTP debug output. The log pipeline scrubs live key prefixes as a backstop. The central log service keeps logs for 30 days. A key value found in a log counts as a new leak, so rotate it again through A3 to A7.

13. A6, confirm every instance is on the new keys. This is a read-only check, run as a saved log query plus a script that looks up the latest store version ids. The security on-call runs the store lookup and the comparison. It passes only when all of these hold:
    - For every pod and every secret, the latest loaded or rotated log line shows the same version id as the latest version in the store.
    - Every A0 consumer is confirmed on the new key or stopped.
    - At least 5 minutes plus a margin have passed since the last store write.
    - No old-image pod remains.
    - Provider error rates are normal.
    If a pod still shows an old version after one more refresh interval, investigate its refresher. Do not revoke.

14. A8 and A9. Before the first revocation, the deploy pipeline must refuse any image built from a commit before the migration commit. Otherwise a rollback would restore a revoked key. A9 is a CI job that fails any change putting an `api_key` in config/*.yaml. It is verified before A5 merges, and false positives are fixed in the rule, never by disabling it.

15. A7, revoke. This starts once A6 passes for that provider's key, A0 shows no consumer on the old key, and A8 is in place. Revoke payments first and watch error rates for 15 minutes. Then do email, then geocoding, with the same gate. Revocation cannot be undone. If errors rise, look for a consumer missed in A0. The recovery is the new key, which is already in the store and in the pods. Never re-enable the old key. Pause the next provider until the cause is known.

16. A10, cleanup. Scan the 30-day logs for the old key values. A hit is handled as an incident, or just recorded if the key is already revoked. Decide what to do with old images (Open question 4). Record revocation times and version ids in the migration log.

17. Local development (R6). `make run` runs R1 against orders-api/dev/* with the developer's identity. `make run --offline` skips R1 and the store. Each provider client points at a local stub server with a fixed dummy key in memory, and `ready` is set at once. If a developer has no dev access, they get a startup error and a non-zero exit. No key files are written to disk.
gaps: Who runs A0, A1, A2, A5, A6 and A7, and who approves the A5 merge, is not stated (Open question 10). The document only says the security on-call performs the A4 writes.

The secret store product is not named. How a pod receives its service identity without an environment credential is also not stated (Open question 11). So I cannot say how R1 authenticates in practice.

It is not stated how non-pod consumers (cron jobs, other services, CI jobs, developer machines) get confirmed on the new key or stopped before A7. Their access to the new key is also undefined, because they have no prod read (Open question 12). A6 and A7 depend on this.
It is not stated how engineers see version ids without reading values for A6, or whether they can (Open question 11).

The deploy tool and image-tag format that records the build commit are unknown (Open question 3). A8, which gates A7, therefore has no concrete mechanism. The document also defines no override and no way for a rollback to get a working key after revocation.

It is not known whether each provider has a read-only auth check for the A4 pre-write validation (Open question 5). Without one, a bad key is caught only at the A5 gate, after some requests may already have failed.

The A5 gate says the 401/403 rate on new pods must be at or below the rate on old pods. It does not give a time window or a number of observations. It also does not say who watches it or what action actually halts the rollout.
It is not stated how the 'migration commit' that A8 uses is identified.
No emergency path is defined for revoking a key early if it is abused before the rollout finishes (Open question 7).
The document does not say whether a staging environment exists (Open question 8). If it does, the main flow would change.
The threshold for the stale-secret alert is not chosen (Open question 9).
How the 'out-of-band refresh' in R3 is triggered, and how it fits with the 5-minute background refresher, is not described in detail.
The document does not say how the app learns the pod identity or name for log lines. It also does not say how many pods an A6 check should expect beyond the '4 pods' stated.
